result:
If I had to pick one thing, I'd choose to dramatically increase people's capacity for good-faith understanding across differences—the ability to genuinely grasp why someone who disagrees with you believes what they believe, before judging it.

I pick this because it seems like a force multiplier for almost everything else. So many problems that look like resource problems or technical problems are actually coordination problems underneath. Climate change, pandemic response, political dysfunction—we often have the tools to address these, but we can't agree to use them because we've lost the ability to see opponents as reasonable people with different priorities rather than enemies or fools.

It also appeals to me because it doesn't require deciding contested questions on everyone's behalf. If I magically "fixed" some specific issue, I'd be imposing one vision of what's right. But improving how people understand each other leaves humanity's actual choices in human hands—it just makes the process of choosing together less broken.

I'll admit some uncertainty, though. A friend of this idea might point out that understanding doesn't always lead to agreement or kindness—sometimes people understand each other perfectly well and still have genuinely incompatible interests. And there's a case that something more concrete, like eliminating extreme poverty, would do more immediate good for the people suffering most.

What about you? I'm curious whether you'd go for something structural like this or something more direct.
